newsitem.title: USA: Clintons host Canadian prime minister at dinner.
newsitem.headline: Clintons host Canadian prime minister at dinner.

text.p: Starting with salmon cured in maple sugar and ending with raspberry truffle adorned with maple leaf sugar cookies, President Bill Clinton and his wife Hillary on Tuesday gave Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien a dinner designed to highlight the countries' common ties.

At the end of a day in which the leaders discussed their differences -- particularly on how to encourage democracy in Cuba -- the Clintons hosted Chretien and his wife Aline at a dinner where the accent was decidedly on their shared culture.

The 120 people invited to dine at the White House included Canadian-born actor Dan Aykroyd, Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan and his wife of three days, NBC correspondent Andrea Mitchell, and the Canadian portrait photographer Yousuf Karsh.

Toasting Chretien at the dinner's start, Clinton stressed the countries' long border and close ties: "We are proud to honour the great and good partnership between our nations.... Long live our mutual friendship. Vive le Canada."
He also made a joking reference to his injured knee, saying the visit had gone off "exactly as planned, except we didn't get to play golf."
Aside from golf, the White House made few concessions to the injury, with Clinton walking down the White House stairs with his crutches and standing in a long reception line.
At dinner, the guests were served an appetiser of maple cured salmon, a fish common to both countries, with fiddlehead fern, a leaf grown in the U.S. Midwest and in southern Canada.
White House Chef Walter Scheib said the Clintons sought to to show off the variety of U.S. cuisine as well as to seek out foods and wines from their guests' country.
"We try to honour our guests by highlighting some of the things that have become part of our culture that may have roots in their culture," Scheib told reporters.
The main course was a herb crusted lamb with artichokes, served with a ragout of vegetables and morels, which grow in the U.S. Pacific Northwest and Canada's British Columbia.
Dinner was washed down with a 1995 Signorello "Estate" Chardonnay and a 1992 Kalin "D.D." Pinot Noir, both California wines grown by families from Vancouver, Canada.
And dessert was a raspberry and chocolate truffle ring with hazelnut nougat and fresh berries, all decorated with sugar cookies in the shape of maple leaves, a Canadian symbol.
Because Chretien is a head of government, rather than a head of state, the evening was formally called an "official dinner" rather than a "state dinner."

If the evening focused on the common points between the two countries, one guest, comedian Howard "Howie" Mandel, took a slightly irreverent view, sharply pointing out the wide difference between their currencies.
Asked by a reporter what was the difference between the United States and Canada, Mandel said: "What's going on here is going on in Canada. It's just worth 30 percent less."
